subject: Agriculture
title: Four-Course Rotation
description: A quick, practical guide to Four-Course Rotation.

hook.text: Leaving fields fallow wastes a third of your land. Charles 'Turnip' Townshend found a way to skip it.

buildup.text: His four-course rotation cycled wheat, turnips, barley, and clover—no fallow year needed.

discovery.text: Clover fixed nitrogen in the soil. Turnips fed livestock through winter. Every acre worked every year.

twist.text: More winter feed meant more animals survived cold months—and more manure to fertilize fields in spring.

climax.text: The cycle reinforced itself: better soil, more crops, more animals, more manure, better soil again.

punchline.text: No wasted year. Every field, every season, pulling its weight.

quiz.question: What was the key benefit of four-course crop rotation?
options: It eliminated the need for fallow years by restoring soil naturally

details.summary: The four-course rotation system developed in 18th-century England eliminated fallow by cycling wheat, turnips, barley, and clover through four fields. This topic covers how this innovation doubled output and helped trigger the British Agricultural Revolution.
details.whyItMatters: By replacing fallow with productive fodder crops, the four-course rotation dramatically increased both crop and livestock output, helping feed the Industrial Revolution's growing urban workforce.
takeaways: The Norfolk four-course system rotated wheat, turnips, barley, and clover
Turnips fed livestock through winter, eliminating the need for autumn slaughter
Clover fixed nitrogen naturally, restoring soil fertility without fallow

faq.question: How did the four-course rotation work?
faq.answer: Fields cycled through wheat (cash grain), turnips (livestock feed and soil cleaning), barley (cash grain), and clover (nitrogen-fixing fodder). Each crop prepared the soil for the next, eliminating the need for unproductive fallow years entirely.

faq.question: Why was eliminating fallow so important for agriculture?
faq.answer: Fallow meant 33–50% of farmland produced nothing each year. Replacing fallow with turnips and clover added both food and animal feed crops, effectively doubling usable farmland and enabling larger livestock herds that provided more manure and meat.
